newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma City bombing trial to get underway.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma City bombing trial to get underway.

text.p: One of the most important criminal trials in U.S. history was to begin on Monday with Gulf War veteran Timothy McVeigh accused of blowing up a federal building in Oklahoma City.

McVeigh, 28, and former army buddy Terry Nichols have been charged with bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995. The blast killed 168 people and injured 500 others and was the worst attack on civilians on U.S. soil.
McVeigh and Nichols, who will be tried at a later date, have both pleaded not guilty. They face the death penalty if convicted.
Tight security surrounded the federal complex in Denver where the first stage of the trial was set to begin on Monday with jury selection.

People were expected to line up to get a prized seat in the courtroom. Twelve seats were set aside for the blast's "victims" -- survivors and family members of those killed -- who travelled here to attend the proceedings.
In Oklahoma City a special closed-circuit telecast, restricted for use by victims, will be viewed at a Federal Aviation Administration facility under tight guard.
Security was high in Denver. Concrete barricades surrounded the city block where the federal courthouse and a federal office building were housed.
Security cameras were positioned, man-hole covers were sealed shut and police ringed the area.

Prosecutors will argue that McVeigh and Nichols harboured anti-government sentiment after an attack by federal agents on the Branch Davidian compound at Waco, Texas, which led to the deaths of about 80 people on April 19, 1993, exactly two years before the Oklahoma City blast.
The defence is expected to argue that the government has the wrong man and that the bombing may have been planned by an unholy alliance of international terrorists that included Iraq and neo-Nazis.
The government has characterised such a possible scenario as fanciful and will argue that McVeigh and Nichols were the masterminds of the plot to bomb the federal building.

The opening day of the long-awaited trial will be a difficult one for the victims, who will be reliving the day of the blast. Nineteen children who were in a day care centre in the federal building were among those killed.

The first task of the trial is to seat an impartial jury. Notices were sent to 1,000 prospective jurors in Denver and 22 surrounding counties, the largest potential pool of jurors in Colorado history.

The potential jurors are expected to be closely questioned on what impact recent pre-trial publicity about purported confessions by McVeigh has had on them. McVeigh's attorneys who have said that their client has not confessed, tried unsucessfully last week to halt the trial. But an appeals court turned them down, paving the way for the trial to begin on Monday.
